name: Wyvern Dust
geological_features: Dune seas of ultra-fine dust particles that behave as fluid in low gravity
Exposed bedrock ridges protruding from the dust like the spines of buried creatures
Electrostatic dust storms that create visible lightning networks
resources: Iron oxide concentrated in bedrock ridges
Rare earth elements in dust particle analysis
description: Wyvern Dust is a small desert world where the surface itself cannot be trusted. The ultra-fine dust that covers ninety percent of the terrain behaves more like liquid than solid in the low gravity, flowing around obstacles, filling depressions, and swallowing anything left stationary for too long. The bedrock ridges that protrude from the dust seas are the only reliable solid ground, their wind-polished surfaces rising in curved spines that give the landscape the appearance of a creature buried just below the surface.

The thin atmosphere does little to moderate temperature extremes but is sufficient to carry the dust in storms of spectacular violence. Electrostatic charge builds rapidly in the moving particles, discharging in continuous lightning networks that illuminate the storm interiors in flickering blue-white. Between storms, the dust settles into a deceptive stillness, its surface appearing firm until pressure reveals it to be meters deep, engulfing equipment and unwary explorers with a speed that borders on predatory.

Wyvern Dust's geology suggests it was once a more substantial world whose surface materials were pulverized by a prolonged period of heavy bombardment. The dust particles are uniform in size and composition, ground to a fineness that implies enormous sustained energy input. The bedrock ridges are the remnants of deeper structures that resisted the pulverization, their compositions older and harder than the surrounding material by billions of years.

Resource extraction on Wyvern Dust is theoretically straightforward but practically hazardous. The dust infiltrates every seal and mechanism, its particles small enough to penetrate standard filters and abrasive enough to destroy bearings and optics. The rare earth content of the dust itself is commercially interesting but separating useful quantities from the bulk material requires processing infrastructure that the environment actively conspires to destroy. Operations here are strictly short-duration, with equipment considered expendable.
